options.text: The courses carry a fixed message set once at building and unchanged by revisits, while the pell stone alone carries a separate, updatable record that passers reset.
Both registers are actually carried by the pell stone, so the unchanged courses simply mean that no one has visited the cairn recently.
The lisk sense records where the route goes and the courses record recent conditions, so it is the builder who updates the pell stone on each revisit.
Since a physical marker's meaning is fixed once it is built, the pell stone's shift must be an incidental disturbance rather than a deliberate update.
Her reasoning is backwards: only the course-to-course cant carries the builder's message; lean, the whole-cairn tilt, is an accidental frost-heave artifact with no meaning.
She is right that the more visually obvious feature carries more meaning — lean is simply a larger-scale version of the same deliberate offset that produces cant.
Her conclusion is wrong for a different reason: the finger's-width course offset is likely an unintentional flaw, so neither feature should be read as a signal.
She has the mechanism right: builders deliberately tilt the whole cairn to reinforce the message already given by a canted course, so both features matter.
Because course three is a single reversed course flanked by agreeing courses, it is a hob: it signals a branch ahead, while the route itself continues east.
It is the same kind of thing as a randomly mis-canted or collapsed course, meaning this cairn is simply poorly built and effectively unreadable to any passer.
A single reversed course lowers the concord score here, and a lower concord always signals a less reliable or worse-built cairn, discounting its message.
It reverses the route: since course three is canted west, the correct reading is that the path itself turns west immediately after this cairn.
The current protocol (Tessaly's, standard since 1986) uses the 0.5 figure because it excludes the crown, whose cant records handling rather than building.
The 0.6 figure reflects the current protocol, since Marhaug's original 1968 definition remains the field's standard reference for surveys today.
Whichever figure is higher must be closer to the truth, since including more courses in an index always makes the summary more accurate.
The crown is excluded from the 0.5 figure for the same reason the footing is: both simply follow the slope of the ground and have no cant of their own.
The local illustrates the Tessaly effect, trusting the courses over a stale stone; the visitor illustrates the Orne effect, misreading a hob as direction.
Both situations illustrate the same phenomenon, since each involves an experienced or inexperienced reader being misled by one feature of the cairn.
The local's choice illustrates the Orne effect, since it involves an experienced reader correctly interpreting a conflicting signal at the cairn.
The visitor's mistake would have been avoided by checking the next cairn, since a stranger taking a wrong direction from a hob should self-correct.
That lean misleads experienced readers more than strangers, since locals judge cant by eye against the vertical rather than course against course.
That locals are fooled by lean because they cannot perceive cant at all, unlike strangers who compare every course individually.
That since strangers misroute more often overall, they must also be more often misled specifically by lean, at a similarly elevated rate.
That experienced readers develop a general immunity to visual distortion, so lean could only ever mislead strangers, never locals.
The claim holds for strangers, whose accuracy rises with concord throughout, but not locals, who read low-concord cairns slightly better — the Marhaug pattern.
The strongest objection is that it is strangers, not locals, who actually read low-concord cairns better, since they aren't anchored by the convention's expectations.
There is no real objection here: guild cairns average lower concord than shepherds' cairns simply because guild builders use more courses overall.
There is no real objection: more agreement among courses is definitionally easier to parse, so any exception would be surveyor error rather than a real pattern.
The cairn has become more readable at the cost of information: the uniform recant erases any hob that flagged a junction, and the reset stone gives a default reading.
Since the conservators followed the standard convention carefully, the restoration should have preserved or even improved the cairn's original information.
The restoration succeeded on both counts: the cairn is now easier to read and at least as informative as the one it replaced, since careful rebuilding preserves intent.
The reset pell stone is effectively broken until someone notices, since a stone placed upslope by conservators cannot carry a genuine reading of its own.
The lisk sense changed when the pell stone was turned; the dorran sense changed only because the courses were physically rebuilt, not because time had simply passed.
Both registers drift with time on their own, so the rebuilt courses and the turned stone are really two instances of the same ordinary aging process.
The pell stone alone carries both registers, so turning it also updated the dorran sense, and the rebuilt courses only mattered because they hold the stone.
Brannagh's objection shows the dorran sense is not truly fixed either, since the builder's original course choices were themselves somewhat arbitrary.
It is a hob: the reversed course does not itself point a direction, but announces that a second route branches off before the next cairn.
The west cant is the message the builder intended: the route turns west immediately after this cairn.
It is an accidental fault, the same kind of course-shift that strangers learn to recognise as unreadable and simply ignore.
The pattern's low resulting concord score means the cairn is unreliable and neither register on it should be trusted.
The first is lean, caused by frost heave under the footing and carrying no meaning; the second is cant, the builder's deliberate offset that points the route's turn.
The first is cant, judged against true vertical the same way lean is; the second is lean, judged course against course rather than against the vertical.
Both measurements are meaningful signals, since any offset a surveyor can measure on a built structure was placed there deliberately.
The first is lean, produced by deliberate builder choice or a heavy pell stone; the second is cant, produced by frost heave under the footing.
The local, because locals judge cant by eye against the vertical silhouette, so the whole-cairn tilt corrupts their reading, while strangers compare each course only to the one beneath it.
The stranger, because expertise should reduce misreading error across the board, so the less experienced reader is always the more vulnerable one.
The local, because locals cannot perceive cant at all and instead rely entirely on the pell stone to judge direction.
The stranger, since strangers already misroute more often overall, so any additional distortion from tilt affects them more too.

It disagrees: Marhaug's original version counts the crown, but the current protocol excludes it, since passers often reset the crown when turning the pell stone, so its cant reflects handling rather than building.
It agrees, since Marhaug's crown-included version remains the one used under the current survey protocol.
It disagrees in the other direction: the crown-excluded version is the older one, since replaced by Marhaug's crown-included version.
It disagrees because the crown is excluded for the same reason the footing is: both merely follow the slope of the ground rather than carry cant.

The Tessaly effect is experienced readers correctly resolving a genuine conflict between courses and a stale-seeming pell stone by trusting the courses; the Orne effect is strangers misreading a hob's reversed course as a direction, with no register conflict at all.
No objection applies: the two are the same effect under different names, since both ultimately involve a reader being misled by the dorran register.
The objection is that the Tessaly effect actually describes strangers being misled by a single reversed course, not experienced locals resolving a register conflict.
The objection is that the Orne effect describes experienced locals misreading a hob, while the Tessaly effect describes strangers, reversing which population each one covers.

Concord is not a uniform quality score: to a stranger it measures overall readability, but to a reader who knows the convention, a reversed course carries information that a smooth run of agreeing courses does not.
Concord should measure readability the same way for any reader, so higher concord ought to help everyone, and the local pattern is most likely sampling noise.
It shows that strangers, not locals, read low-concord cairns better, since strangers are not anchored by conventional expectations about how a cairn should look.
It shows that low concord specifically signals a nearby junction for guild-built cairns, which is why guild cairns average lower concord than shepherds' cairns.

Restoration trades informativeness for readability: laying every course to agree erases any hob marking a junction, and resetting the pell stone overwrites what recent walkers had recorded, so the rebuilt cairn says less than the one it replaced.
No objection applies: faithful restoration should preserve or improve a marker's information, since more consistent construction only adds clarity for future readers.
The objection is that restoration makes a cairn both easier to read and more informative at once, since consistent construction improves both registers together.
The objection is that the reset pell stone is simply broken until a passer notices and fixes it, rather than a working part of the lisk register.
